featured_reviews.name: Amisha J
featured_reviews.review_text:
I bought a pair of Neeman’s shoes on 30th August from the R City store, reassured several times by both the manager and attendant that “if there’s any problem, just bring them back.” Well, there was a problem. Within 15 minutes of wearing them at home to break in, my toe went numb. So I did what any reasonable customer would do — I went back on 5th September to exchange them for a bigger size or return them for a more fitting pair. That’s when the story flipped.

The same store that promised an easy exchange suddenly declared the shoes “not resalable” because they had been “used.” Really? A grand total of 20 minutes between the store and home counts as “used”? Apparently Neeman’s expects customers to magically know whether their shoes will hurt without ever actually wearing them. Brilliant.

Instead of helping, the manager got worked up and said he’d “send an email ahead” and update me in two days. It’s been four now, with radio silence. While leaving the store, I had to remind them to take pictures of the shoes, because apparently the burden of “justifying” their refusal falls entirely on the customer.

So here’s what I wonder now:
1. If the manager was so sure they weren’t resalable, why did he need to email someone else to confirm?
2. If he has no authority and must email, shouldn’t he attach the proof without the customer reminding him? Unless of course, his boss is clairvoyant.
3. If the shoes show so much “damage” after 20 minutes of wear, will they even last two days?

What should have been a simple, straightforward exchange has turned into a drawn-out ordeal. At this point, I don’t want a replacement; not now, not ever in the future. I want my refund.

So here we are: a brand that loudly boasts eco-friendly values but has no problem wasting a perfectly new pair of shoes because they won’t stand by their own word. Neeman’s talks big about sustainability, but what they actually deliver is broken promises, disappointing service, and a wasted product. If this is their version of “responsibility,” I’d strongly recommend saving yourself the headache and shopping elsewhere (Psst! Skechers).

PS: If you really want the unfiltered reviews about this brand - head to Reddit. I wish I had before buying.

Edit 09/10/2025: I was contacted by the Cluster Manager, who suggested a solution. I wouldn’t have minded if the return was outright refused, but the way the store handled the situation was frustrating, delayed responses, lack of professionalism, and poor communication turned a simple exchange into an ordeal. That said, I must mention manager Mr. Sham Chavan, who handled the situation professionally and patiently, explaining the issue clearly. The experience highlights a serious gap in store-level service, even when the product itself may be ok.

Great for old‑season originals at big discounts, but be careful with clothes.

I came from Gujarat tovisit sooper buy in Ghatkopar to buy some shoes, and overall I’d say it’s a good spot if you don’t mind old‑season models and are okay with doing a bit of searching. The collection is kind of mid‑range: most of the shoes are older models, and the majority of brands on display are Puma, mostly in white canvas style. The shoes are 100% original for the brands they show, which is a big plus. If you negotiate well, they can give you around 65–70% discount on the MRP, so it’s worth bargaining and pushing a bit.
The clothes section is a bit mixed — I noticed some first‑copy items mixed in with the originals, so I’m not fully sure about the authenticity of all the apparel. If you’re looking for clothes, I’d suggest checking the quality carefully.
If you’re okay with older models, a self‑serve‑style shopping experience, and don’t mind inspecting items yourself, Superbuy is worth a visit for good deals on original‑brand shoes.

My experience at this shop was very disappointing. I bought a pair of JoyBean brand sandals for ₹1,500. The shopkeeper initially quoted ₹1,900, and after bargaining, I purchased them for ₹1,500. However, when I returned home and checked the brand’s official website, I found that the MRP was ₹1,399 and the selling price was ₹1,245. Moreover, the original price tag had been removed from the item.

It appears that inflating the price first and then reducing it during bargaining is a tactic used to make customers feel satisfied, while still giving the shopkeeper an unfair advantage.

This practice is misleading and unfair. I advise others to avoid such fraudulent shops. If you do visit, make sure to check the price tag and do not fall for the shopkeeper’s sweet talk.
